tags.gist: Reports CMS and seven state coverage regimes place the AI duty on the regulated user, never the developer, reaching suppliers only through regulated entities.
Offers a three-question drafting test for any accountability assignment: is the bearer named, does satisfaction act on proof or duty, is the trigger direction-neutral.
Summarizes that coverage law reaches model suppliers only through the regulated entity, offering three consistent mechanisms and one way such a mechanism fails.
Says state law shows clinician supervision means different things in different settings, and reduces the record to a test for drafting postmarket roles.
Offers coverage-decision law, where payers are named ecosystem participants, as a domestic record of who answers when software joins a patient decision.
Would add a dimension beside downstream safeguards: whether the legal requirement for a safeguard can be discharged without actually performing it.
Contrasts Colorado, where supervision attaches to a responsible provider, with Alabama, where attestation satisfies the human-decision duty, placing one device at different axis positions.
Suggests the framework acknowledge the supervised position as dependent on whether supervision is enforceable in the deployment setting's governing law.
Would keep time pressure as an explicit modifier, since supervision that must happen within seconds may exist in name only.
Describes two enforceable state answers: Texas prohibits automated adverse determinations, while Colorado allocates duty to the insurer even when vendors are used.
Argues allocation of responsibility outlasts prohibition as models improve, making it the more durable design for a postmarket framework.
Shows how a discharge clause undoes allocation: Alabama's act lets attested reliance on vendors satisfy the duty itself, unlike narrower proof provisions elsewhere.
Says assigning a role and defining its discharge are separate choices; stakeholder roles should be inputs the manufacturer acts on, not substitute duties.
Casts clinicians as reporters of fluent, plausible, wrong outputs seen in use; such a report is a postmarket signal, not transferred accountability.
Says institutions owning the deployment environment can preserve logs and notify manufacturers of local configuration changes, but should not re-validate the model.
Sees professional societies and standards bodies as natural authors for shared competency batteries and incident taxonomies.
Notes state rules restrict denials but never automated approvals, so a rule written for one error direction leaves the other direction unregulated.
Suggests postmarket role triggers attach to the system's use in a decision, not to which way its outcome went.
Reviews coverage law: duties fall on the regulated user, suppliers appear only through that duty, and self-funded plans and practice remain untested.
Proposes supplier information be required through the manufacturer's quality-system purchasing controls, with suppliers producing sensitive material directly to FDA on authorization.
Warns that supplier production should demonstrate compliance, never count as satisfying the manufacturer's own obligation, or it repeats Alabama's flaw.
Says evaluating the assembled device and using the premarket baseline to detect and re-check developer-initiated changes avoids making developers manufacturers.
Accepts a voluntary master file as reducing duplicate review, but says it cannot replace the manufacturer's showing after an uninitiated change, and incentives remain weak.
Says a PCCP may govern the response to a class of upstream changes but cannot stand in for supplier information duties and device-level evaluation.
Notes Maryland's most categorical prohibition names no bearer, leaving no one to monitor or report, while designation quality and enforceability remain independent.
Reduces the record to three drafting questions, bearer named, satisfaction acting on proof, direction-neutral trigger, applicable to CDRH's own role assignments.
